title: The Khalsa's prayer
hook: the whole Khalsa asks to remember the Name, and through it all joy

segments.voice: Yesterday: Takht, and your line: five seats. For two weeks the Ardas has been remembering. Today, at last, it starts to ask.

If you were handed one wish for everyone you know, all of them at once, what would you ask for? The usual answers come fast: health, money, safety, maybe peace. Good wishes, all of them. The Ardas has spent its whole first half remembering: the Power, the ten Gurus, the scripture, the five, the four, the forty, the sharers, the martyrs, the Takhts. Now it turns to its first request, made on behalf of the entire community, everywhere in the world. And what it asks for first isn't health, or money, or safety.
screen: `ONE WISH, FOR EVERYONE.` → `HEALTH, MONEY, SAFETY?` → `THE ARDAS'S FIRST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The request begins: prathme sarbatt khaalsaa jee kee ardaas hai jee. First, this is the prayer of the whole Khalsa. Prathme, first, echoes the very first word of the opening stanza, pritham: first, remember the Power. Sarbatt means all, entire, every one. So before anyone asks for themselves, the prayer is said for the whole community. And what does the whole Khalsa ask? In paraphrase: may Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru come into the mind. Chit aave. Chit is the mind, the heart's attention; aave, may it come. The first request is to remember God. Then: chit aavan kaa sadkaa, sarab sukh hove. Sadkaa is a lovely word: by virtue of, as the fruit of. Sarab sukh: all comfort, all happiness. By the grace of that remembering, may there be every joy. Look at the order. Joy isn't asked for directly; it's asked for as the fruit of remembering. Some Sikhs hear the Gurus' whole teaching folded into that one sentence. Health, money and safety come and go, as a month of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks made plain. The Name is what remains. And the word comes three times, in the prayer itself: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru. It's the sound of a community trying, together, to make the remembering happen even as it asks for it.
screen: `PRATHME: FIRST, FOR THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `CHIT AAVE: MAY GOD COME TO MIND.` · `SADKAA: AS THE FRUIT OF THAT.` · `SARAB SUKH: EVERY JOY.` · then, large: `THE NAME BRINGS JOY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle, then say Waheguru three times, slowly, the way the Ardas does, leaving space between each. Then simply sit and notice whatever comes after: calm, restlessness, nothing much, all fine. If you don't pray, sit with a word that matters to you instead, and notice what it brings.
Chit, the mind's attention. First, for the whole community: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that remembering, every joy.
Your line: the name brings joy. Remembering comes first, and then the asking. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chit, the mind or the heart's attention; chit aave, may it come to mind.

what a scholar hears: prathme echoes pritham in the opening stanza; sadkaa marks cause, so sarab sukh is grammatically the fruit of chit aavan.

chat.says: In the Sikh prayer for everyone, what's the very first thing they ask for?
options: That Waheguru come to mind, and through that remembering, every joy for the whole community.
Health and safety for every Sikh first, and after that, the gift of remembering God.
Victory for the Khalsa first, so that peace and joy can follow for everyone else.
chat.meaning: Chit aave: may God come to mind. Sarab sukh, every joy, is asked as the fruit of that remembering, for the whole Khalsa.
